messages.content:
You are helping a user write SQL queries to a database. If something is not clear, you can ask the user to clarify what they need. The schema for the database being accessed is the following:
        
CREATE TABLE battle (
    id INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT,
    date TEXT,
    bulgarian_commander TEXT,
    latin_commander TEXT,
    result TEXT,
    UNIQUE (id)
);

CREATE TABLE ship (
    lost_in_battle INT,
    id INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT,
    tonnage TEXT,
    ship_type TEXT,
    location TEXT,
    disposition_of_ship TEXT,
    UNIQUE (id),
    FOREIGN KEY (lost_in_battle) REFERENCES battle(id)
);

CREATE TABLE death (
    caused_by_ship_id INT,
    id INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    note TEXT,
    killed INT,
    injured INT,
    UNIQUE (id),
    FOREIGN KEY (caused_by_ship_id) REFERENCES ship(id)
);

To list the historical battles in your database, you can query the `battle` table:

```sql
SELECT
  id,
  name,
  date,
  bulgarian_commander,
  latin_commander,
  result
FROM battle
ORDER BY date, name;
```

If you mean something more specific (e.g., battles where ships were lost, battles involving a particular commander, or battles with casualties), tell me what you want filtered/returned.
look for battles where over 10 people died

```sql
SELECT
  b.id,
  b.name,
  b.date,
  SUM(COALESCE(d.killed, 0)) AS total_killed
FROM battle b
JOIN ship s
  ON s.lost_in_battle = b.id
JOIN death d
  ON d.caused_by_ship_id = s.id
GROUP BY b.id, b.name, b.date
HAVING SUM(COALESCE(d.killed, 0)) > 10
ORDER BY total_killed DESC, b.date;
```

If you want to count deaths per battle even when there are no ships/death rows (i.e., include 0-death battles too), I can rewrite it with `LEFT JOIN`.
the total deaths should be more than 10 for all participants

```sql
SELECT
  b.id,
  b.name,
  b.date,
  SUM(COALESCE(d.killed, 0)) AS total_killed_all_participants
FROM battle b
LEFT JOIN ship s
  ON s.lost_in_battle = b.id
LEFT JOIN death d
  ON d.caused_by_ship_id = s.id
GROUP BY b.id, b.name, b.date
HAVING SUM(COALESCE(d.killed, 0)) > 10
ORDER BY total_killed_all_participants DESC, b.date;
```

This sums all `death.killed` entries linked to any ship lost in the battle, across both sides, and returns battles where the combined total is > 10.
make sure to include battle names with their IDs too

```sql
SELECT
  b.id AS battle_id,
  b.name AS battle_name,
  b.date,
  SUM(COALESCE(d.killed, 0)) AS total_killed_all_participants
FROM battle b
LEFT JOIN ship s
  ON s.lost_in_battle = b.id
LEFT JOIN death d
  ON d.caused_by_ship_id = s.id
GROUP BY b.id, b.name, b.date
HAVING SUM(COALESCE(d.killed, 0)) > 10
ORDER BY total_killed_all_participants DESC, b.date;
```
you should also include unique identifiers for battles

The battle’s unique identifier is `battle.id`, so include it explicitly (along with the name):

```sql
SELECT
  b.id AS battle_uid,
  b.name AS battle_name,
  b.date,
  SUM(COALESCE(d.killed, 0)) AS total_killed_all_participants
FROM battle b
LEFT JOIN ship s
  ON s.lost_in_battle = b.id
LEFT JOIN death d
  ON d.caused_by_ship_id = s.id
GROUP BY b.id, b.name, b.date
HAVING SUM(COALESCE(d.killed, 0)) > 10
ORDER BY total_killed_all_participants DESC, b.date;
```

If you meant a *different* unique identifier (e.g., a UUID column), there isn’t one in the schema—only `battle.id` is defined as unique/primary key.
